headline: AI-generated women posing as stand-up comics on Instagram have copied the routines of eight real comedians, WIRED found, and Meta has told at least one of them the copying does not break its rules.
score_reason: Pool score kept: WIRED's own reporting on a real creator problem with a platform-policy and copyright gap, but the harm is mostly to a small group of comedians.
importance_line: Comedians and other creators lose credit and income when their work is copied wholesale, viewers may not be able to tell what is real, and Instagram's rules cover impersonation and unlabelled AI content but not copying material that is not copyrighted, such as jokes, so the gap sits in platform policy and copyright law.
summary: WIRED reports that it identified eight stand-up comedians whose videos were copied by scantily dressed, AI-generated women on Instagram, at least two of the accounts linking to adult subscription pages, and that Julia Jasunas, a stand-up comedian, says Meta, Instagram's parent company, told her the copy of her joke did not break its rules because the account was not pretending to be her. Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, told another comedian, George Brett Olson, that banning AI content is not practical but that Instagram wants to send more traffic to original creators, and WIRED notes that jokes have little copyright protection, so comedians have few options.
notes: Read in full on wired.com (published 16 Oct 2026). WIRED's own reporting; the accounts named (Aylen Skye, Tiffany Sloane) did not comment to WIRED, one removed a video after a comedian's post, and a Meta spokesperson, Francis Brennan, declined to comment beyond saying Meta's policies are clear. Olson's viral post about the copying was on 3 Oct 2026. WIRED's 'eight comics' is the number it found, not a full count.
